values.P_heading: Work-up and reporting descriptors do not explain the offsets
values.P_sentence: However, adding the parsed work-up and reporting descriptors (P) did not significantly reduce the error for unseen studies for either target after Holm correction.
values.P_all_learners_sentence: On the locked test studies, P significantly reduced per-study RMSE for 0 and significantly increased it for 0 of the 24 learner–target combinations (Holm-corrected Wilcoxon tests).
values.kw_sentence: Kruskal–Wallis *p* = 0.104 for bio-oil; Kruskal–Wallis *p* = 0.951 for solids
values.ea_sentence: The most negative median offset for bio-oil occurred for studies using ethyl acetate (median offset -12.7 wt%, 7 studies), but such groups are small and the differences were not significant.
values.gen_cov_sentence: and on the locked test studies (bio-oil RC 0.60 vs SC 0.89; solids RC 0.46 vs SC 0.82), for left-out feedstock families (mean) (bio-oil RC 0.55 vs SC 0.89; solids RC 0.60 vs SC 0.90), for temporally later studies (bio-oil RC 0.42 vs SC 0.85; solids RC 0.56 vs SC 0.90), on the external hydrochar database (solids RC 0.55 vs SC 0.92).
values.kshot_eb_sentence: Shrinkage lowered the per-study RMSE relative to the raw mean offset at k = 1, 2, 3, 5, 10 (Holm-corrected Wilcoxon, bio-oil) and was never significantly worse.
values.tuning_sentence: Replacing the tuned hyper-parameters of the base learner by library defaults changed its study-grouped RMSE by 0.0–1.0 wt% (Supplementary Table S7), so the conclusions do not hinge on tuning.
values.tau2_sentence: Estimating $\tau^2$ by restricted maximum likelihood instead of the method of moments gave median per-study RMSE at k = 1 of 9.37 vs 10.06 wt% (bio-oil) and 9.33 vs 8.89 wt% (solids; Supplementary Table S6).
values.adaptive_main_sentence: An exploratory, post-hoc variant with locally adaptive widths (Supplementary Section S4) did not narrow the intervals (mean width 63.0 vs 59.1 wt% for bio-oil) and worsened the interval score, consistent with an error dominated by an unpredictable study offset.
values.locked_paragraph: The locked test studies, evaluated once after all modelling decisions had been frozen, gave a more pessimistic picture than development CV. For bio-oil yield (556 runs, 28 studies) the STRATA base learner reached RMSE = 18.3 wt% (R² = -0.95; best learner k-nearest neighbours, 12.9 wt%; mean predictor 13.6 wt%); for solid yield (457 runs, 30 studies) the STRATA base learner reached RMSE = 18.5 wt% (R² = 0.30; best learner MLP, 14.4 wt%; mean predictor 23.0 wt%). For bio-oil, only 4 of the 11 non-trivial learners had a lower pooled RMSE than the mean predictor, although 6 had a lower median per-study RMSE: pooled errors were dominated by a few studies outside the bulk of the training distribution — for XGBoost, a single solvothermal series of 90 runs contributed 54% of the squared error, and excluding it (post hoc) lowered the RMSE from 18.3 to 13.6 wt% (R² = 0.00). Study-weighted coverage of row-calibrated 90% intervals was 0.60 (95% CI 0.47–0.73) for bio-oil and 0.46 (95% CI 0.34–0.58) for solids; study-calibrated intervals reached 0.89 (95% CI 0.81–0.97) and 0.82 (95% CI 0.70–0.92) (Table 6, Fig. 5). Study calibration thus removed most, but for solids not all, of the under-coverage; with 28–30 locked studies the intervals are wide, and the solid-yield shortfall reflects a few studies with feedstocks (technical lignin, plastic–biomass blends) that are rare in the training data.
values.abstract_locked_sentence: On 38 locked studies, study-calibrated intervals covered 0.89 (bio-oil) and 0.82 (solids) of runs, versus 0.60 and 0.46 for row-calibrated intervals, and no learner predicted bio-oil yields of new studies substantially better than the training mean.
values.hl_cov: Study-calibrated intervals raised coverage from 0.46–0.61 to 0.82–0.91
values.generalisation_paragraph: Predicting studies published after 2018 from earlier studies gave RMSE = 19.4 (bio-oil; higher than the study-grouped CV value of 15.8 wt%) and 16.5 wt% (solids; higher than 14.1 wt%), i.e. models trained on older literature transfer no better to newer studies than to randomly chosen unseen studies. Leaving out one feedstock family at a time gave mean RMSE of 17.2 and 16.3 wt%, with the largest errors for the 'Other' category (bio-oil, 32.6 wt%) and 'Other' (solids, 29.8 wt%). On the independent 4TU hydrochar database (502 runs after removing 36 potential duplicates; 69 feedstock series), a solid-yield model trained on all development studies reached RMSE = 13.3 wt% (R² = 0.31), whereas training on the 16 HTC development studies alone gave 16.7 wt% (R² = -0.08), showing that the small HTC subset of the primary database does not by itself support transfer to other HTC compilations (Table 7).
values.robustness_paragraph: Adding Gaussian noise of 20% of the training standard deviation to continuous test features increased the bio-oil RMSE from 15.7 to 16.6 wt% and the solid RMSE from 13.9 to 15.4 wt%, while SC coverage was 0.90 without and 0.90 with noise (bio-oil) — the error budget for unseen studies is dominated by the study offset, not by input noise. Training on 25% instead of all training studies raised the bio-oil RMSE from 15.7 to 20.3 wt%, and SC coverage remained 0.89, whereas RC coverage stayed at 0.45–0.56 (Fig. 7).
values.efficiency_paragraph: All learners trained in at most 9 s on one CPU thread (MLP); the STRATA base learner took 0.2 s and predicted 1,000 runs in 4 ms (Table 8, Fig. 8). The complete STRATA procedure — two inner five-fold cross-validations, quantiles, variance components and k-shot quantiles for all k — took 2.3–7.0 s on all development studies, against 0.3–0.5 s for fitting the base learner alone (measured, 1 and 4 threads); this overhead is negligible compared with the cost of a single hydrothermal experiment.
values.error_paragraph: Out-of-study errors were largest for Other feedstocks among families (bio-oil RMSE 33.9 wt%, 6 studies), for the ≤250 °C temperature band (21.1 wt%) and for HTL solvothermal runs (18.5 wt%) (Supplementary Table S9). The five worst-predicted bio-oil studies had per-study RMSE between 35.1 and 61.4 wt% and absolute mean offsets of 26.7–60.9 wt% (processes: HTL 3, HTC 1, HTL solvothermal 1). Across extraction-solvent groups with at least three studies, the bio-oil RMSE ranged from 10.8 (hydrocarbon) to 19.8 wt% (none named) and the mean residual from -9.5 to +9.7 wt% (Fig. 9).
values.adaptive_sentence: For bio-oil, SC-N gave study-weighted coverage 0.91 (SC 0.91) with median width 55.6 vs 59.5 wt% and mean interval score 84.2 vs 77.3; for solids, coverage 0.92 vs 0.91, median width 53.3 vs 45.7 wt%, interval score 69.5 vs 65.2. The adaptive variant therefore did not improve interval efficiency — both widths and interval scores were worse — although coverage across process subtypes became more uniform (largest deviation from 0.90: 0.03 vs 0.07 for solids). This negative result is consistent with the main finding that the dominant error component is a study offset that input features cannot localise. Because this variant was added after inspecting pipeline-verification results, it is reported as exploratory and is not part of the main claims.
